title: Trade Policy Activity Index
text:
Trade Policy Activity Index
    
    
    
      A novel composite indicator measuring the evolution of global trade policy
      since the Global Financial Crisis, covering 197 countries and territories.
    
  







  
    About the TPA Index

    
      The Trade Policy Activity (TPA) Index is a novel monthly indicator of global trade
      policy dynamics covering 197 countries and territories since the Global Financial
      Crisis. Built using a Dynamic Factor Model on data from the WTO Trade Monitoring
      Database and the Global Trade Alert, the Index reveals a rising trend with distinct
      peaks at the 2018–2019 and 2025 trade tensions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the war
      in Ukraine. It complements existing trade uncertainty and geopolitical risk measures
      while capturing substantial additional trade-policy variation.
    

    
      
        How has it been constructed?
        
          A Dynamic Factor Model (DFM) extracts the common component of policy variation
          across measure categories and two complementary sources: the WTO Trade Monitoring
          Database and the Global Trade Alert. The model treats policy records as imperfect
          signals of latent global trade policy activity, with weights determined endogenously
          from the data. A trend-cycle decomposition distinguishes structural shifts from
          cyclical fluctuations, while a block structure separates the global signal from
          category-specific variation. All series are smoothed using a three-month moving
          average and normalized to mean zero over January 2010–December 2011.
        
      
      
        What does it include?
        
          The dataset provides eight monthly series from January 2010 to October 2025:
          a Global Factor (the baseline worldwide index);
          a Facilitating sub-index (trade-facilitating measures, including
          rollbacks); an Other sub-index (non-facilitating measures —
          tariff increases, bans, quotas, subsidies);
          a Restrictive sub-index (trade-restricting subset of Other,
          following Deardorff 2014); a Remaining other sub-index (the residual,
          largely subsidies); G20 and Non-G20 indices; and a
          GDP-weighted index using pre-sample GDP shares (2005–2009) as
          time-invariant weights. Sheet 1 provides normalized indices; Sheet 2 the unnormalized
          global factor.
        
      
    

    
      
        Why is it different from other measures?
        
          Existing measures capture important but partial dimensions: news-based indices track
          uncertainty and geopolitical risk through media coverage, while welfare-based indices
          measure trade restrictiveness at the country level. The TPA tracks a different
          dimension — the flow of actual policy changes at monthly frequency, across a
          comprehensive set of instruments, covering both facilitating and restrictive measures
          globally. The DFM extracts underlying co-movement across diverse instruments rather
          than counting interventions or relying on news coverage. Cointegration tests confirm
          that the TPA shares a long-run relationship with each existing measure while
          capturing substantial independent variation — even relative to the most closely
          related index, roughly half of the TPA's variation is distinct.
        
      
      
        What are the key findings?
        
          The Index reveals a rising trend that accelerates from 2020 onward, with distinct
          peaks at the US–China tariff escalation (2018–2019), the COVID-19 pandemic (2020),
          the war in Ukraine (2022), and renewed trade tensions in 2025. Facilitating and
          restrictive measures co-move strongly during crises — countries restrict exports of
          scarce goods while easing imports of essentials — but diverge sharply during the
          2018–2019 and 2025 trade tensions, when restrictive measures accelerated and
          facilitating measures decelerated. The 2025 spike is driven predominantly by tariffs
          and export controls, while subsidies and other distortive measures show the most
          broad-based increase throughout the sample. G20 economies exhibit sharper peaks in
          2018–2019 and 2025; non-G20 economies recorded larger COVID-19 spikes. Excluding the
          US and China shows the rise in restrictive measures since 2022 extends well beyond
          the two largest economies.
